Personal lines insurance makes up the bulk of most people's direct experience with the industry.

terms.definition: Insurance products tailored to an individual's specific risk profile and preferences, using data analytics and machine learning to customize pricing and coverage rather than relying on broad rating categories. This approach represents a meaningful shift away from broad rating classes toward pricing that reflects an individual's actual, specific risk profile as closely as the available data allows.
examples: Personalized insurance priced her policy based on her own driving data, not just her age and zip code.
The insurer's personalized insurance offering adjusted coverage recommendations as circumstances changed.
Personalized insurance depends on collecting more individual data than traditional underwriting required.
Personalized insurance pricing can reward low-risk individuals with meaningfully lower premiums.
Some customers were uneasy about how much data personalized insurance required them to share.

terms.definition: The software system an insurer uses to manage policies and related processes, including underwriting, billing, and claims, increasingly integrating AI and analytics to improve efficiency. A well-integrated system like this reduces manual work and errors across the policy lifecycle, from initial issuance through renewal and eventual cancellation.
examples: The new policy administration system cut the time it took to issue an endorsement from days to minutes.
Migrating to a modern policy administration system was the company's biggest technology project in years.
The policy administration system flagged a billing discrepancy before it reached the customer.
Every underwriting decision eventually flowed through the policy administration system.
An outdated policy administration system limited how quickly the insurer could launch new products.

terms.definition: A ratio measuring an insurer's financial leverage by comparing net written premiums to policyholders' surplus, indicating the insurer's ability to absorb above-average losses. A high ratio can signal an insurer is writing more business relative to its financial cushion than is prudent, making this a key metric regulators and rating agencies watch closely.
examples: A rising premium to surplus ratio signaled the insurer was writing more business relative to its capital cushion.
Rating agencies watch the premium to surplus ratio closely when reviewing financial strength.
The premium to surplus ratio stayed within the range regulators consider healthy.
A high premium to surplus ratio can mean an insurer is more exposed to a bad loss year.
The company raised additional capital partly to bring its premium to surplus ratio back in line.

terms.definition: A component of cyber liability insurance covering costs associated with data breaches, including legal fees, regulatory fines, and customer notification expenses tied to mishandling personal data. It addresses the liability exposure specifically tied to mishandling personal data, complementing the more operational, first-party costs covered under data breach insurance.
examples: Privacy liability insurance covered the regulatory fine after the data protection violation.
The company's privacy liability insurance paid for notifying every customer affected by the breach.
Privacy liability insurance is increasingly important as data protection regulations grow stricter.
The underwriter reviewed the company's data handling practices before quoting privacy liability insurance.
Privacy liability insurance and network security liability insurance are often sold together as parts of one cyber policy.

terms.definition: A broad category of insurance covering property losses (home, car, other possessions) and liability for accidents or damage caused to others, as opposed to life and health insurance. This is the traditional two-branch structure underlying most of the general insurance industry, distinct from the separate life and health insurance sector, which addresses very different kinds of risk.
examples: The company wrote both property and casualty insurance and life insurance, in separate divisions.
P&C insurance includes everything from homeowners to commercial general liability policies.
Property and casualty insurance results are more exposed to catastrophe losses than life insurance is.
She spent her whole career in property and casualty insurance underwriting.
P&C insurance premiums are typically shorter-term than the multi-decade contracts common in life insurance.

terms.definition: The use of mathematical and statistical methods to evaluate financial and risk variables in insurance, including risk assessment, pricing models, and the valuation of complex financial instruments. This kind of rigorous, mathematical approach underlies much of modern actuarial work, from setting rates to valuing complex investment holdings on an insurer's balance sheet.
examples: Quantitative analysis supported the actuary's recommendation to adjust the pricing model.
The reinsurance team relied on quantitative analysis to value a complex structured treaty.
Quantitative analysis increasingly draws on machine learning alongside traditional statistics.
A quantitative analysis of the loss data revealed a seasonal pattern worth pricing for.
Quantitative analysis is only as good as the assumptions and data feeding into it.

terms.definition: The process of determining insurance premiums based on risk assessment and statistical data, analyzing historical trends to set prices sufficient to cover projected claims, expenses, and profit. It's the practical, applied process that turns loss cost, expense load, and other pricing components into the actual rates an insurer files and charges.
examples: Rate making for the new product relied heavily on industry loss data, since the insurer had none of its own yet.
The rate making process had to balance competitiveness against long-term profitability.
Regulators reviewed the insurer's rate making methodology before approving the new rates.
Rate making got more precise once telematics data became available as an input.
A rate making error that undercharges for risk can take years to fully show up in results.

terms.definition: The use of satellite or aerial imagery to collect information about objects or areas from a distance, applied in insurance to assess risk, manage claims, and understand environmental factors affecting a policy. This technology lets insurers gather information about a property or area without needing an on-site visit, which is especially valuable for assessing risk or damage across a wide or hard-to-reach area.
examples: Remote sensing technology assessed crop damage across the whole farm without a single site visit.
The insurer used remote sensing technology to check roof condition ahead of renewal.
Remote sensing technology helped estimate the scale of damage right after the wildfire, before adjusters could get in.
Remote sensing technology is especially useful for agricultural and natural catastrophe insurance.
Combining remote sensing technology with historical claims data sharpened the insurer's flood risk maps.

terms.definition: The percentage of net premiums written compared to gross premiums written, showing how much premium risk an insurer keeps after reinsurance rather than ceding away. A lower ratio indicates an insurer is ceding a larger share of its business to reinsurers, while a higher ratio means it's retaining more risk, and correspondingly more premium, for its own account.
examples: A high retention ratio suggested the insurer was relying less on reinsurance than its peers.
The retention ratio dropped after the company bought more reinsurance following a bad loss year.
Analysts used the retention ratio to gauge how much risk the insurer was comfortable keeping.
Retention ratio and net written premium tend to move together for a given book of business.
The reinsurance renewal negotiation directly shaped next year's retention ratio.

terms.definition: A measure of profitability showing how much profit a company generates relative to shareholders' invested capital, used in insurance to judge how efficiently an insurer deploys its capital. Insurers and investors use this figure to compare how efficiently different companies convert shareholder capital into actual profit, independent of the companies' differing sizes.
examples: A strong underwriting year lifted the insurer's return on equity well above its usual range.
Investors compared ROE across insurers to judge which used capital most efficiently.
The insurer's ROE target factored into decisions about how much business to write in a soft market.
A high ROE can come from either strong profits or unusually thin capital, so context matters.
Return on equity is one of the headline numbers analysts look at in an insurer's annual report.

terms.definition: Analytical models used to evaluate the probability and impact of risks. Advanced risk assessment models increasingly incorporate AI and machine learning to improve the accuracy of risk evaluations and premium calculations. As these models incorporate more sophisticated data and techniques, they've become central to how insurers move beyond broad, traditional rating factors toward more precise, individualized risk evaluation.
examples: The new risk assessment model outperformed the old one on every backtest the team ran.
Risk assessment models combined traditional actuarial data with newer telematics inputs.
The regulator asked the insurer to explain how its risk assessment models reached certain conclusions.
Risk assessment models need regular recalibration as underlying conditions change.
A flawed risk assessment model can systematically underprice an entire book of business.

terms.definition: The practice of spreading financial risk across a large number of contributors, letting an insurer cover large individual losses using contributions from all policyholders rather than any one person bearing the full cost. This is the same fundamental mechanism, grounded in the law of large numbers, that makes insurance viable in the first place, regardless of the specific line of business involved.
examples: Risk pooling is the basic mechanism that makes insurance affordable for any single policyholder.
A larger pool made risk pooling more stable, since losses averaged out across more people.
Risk pooling breaks down if too many high-risk individuals join and too few low-risk ones do.
The mutual company's whole structure was built around risk pooling among its members.
Reinsurance is itself a form of risk pooling, spread across insurers rather than individuals.

terms.definition: The use of sensor devices and IoT technology to collect data on insured assets or risks, enabling real-time monitoring for health, auto, and property insurance to support more accurate risk assessment and loss prevention. This real-time monitoring capability shifts insurance from a purely reactive, after-the-loss model toward one that can also help prevent losses before they happen.
examples: Sensor technology in insurance detected the water leak hours before it would have caused major damage.
The pilot program used sensor technology in insurance to monitor temperature in a cold-storage warehouse.
Sensor technology in insurance turned a once-a-year inspection into continuous monitoring.
Wearable sensor technology in insurance let a health insurer offer activity-based discounts.
Sensor technology in insurance raised new questions about how long collected data should be kept.

terms.definition: Insurance products designed for the sharing economy, where assets and services are shared between individuals through a digital platform, covering hosts, guests, drivers, and renters. It addresses a genuine coverage gap, since standard personal auto or homeowners policies often exclude commercial use of a shared vehicle or property, leaving participants unintentionally uninsured without this specific coverage.
examples: Sharing economy insurance covered the host's liability when a guest was injured on the property.
The ride-share driver relied on sharing economy insurance to fill the gap her personal auto policy didn't cover.
Sharing economy insurance often only applies while the platform's app is actively in use.
Sharing economy insurance had to be built quickly as the underlying platforms grew faster than traditional products.
Sharing economy insurance adapts standard coverage concepts to a much shorter, more intermittent kind of exposure.

terms.definition: A reserve an insurance company is legally required to maintain, set by regulation, to help ensure the insurer can meet its future obligations to policyholders. It's the regulatory-mandated counterpart to an insurer's own internally calculated reserves, ensuring a baseline level of financial protection regardless of a company's internal assumptions.
examples: The insurer's statutory reserve calculation followed the formula set by the state regulator.
A shortfall in the statutory reserve would have triggered regulatory intervention.
Statutory reserve requirements are typically more conservative than an insurer's own internal reserve estimate.
The actuary certified that the statutory reserve met the minimum required by law.
Statutory reserve rules differ somewhat from one jurisdiction to the next.

terms.definition: Processing insurance policies or claims entirely electronically, from start to finish, without manual intervention, improving efficiency, reducing processing time, and minimizing errors. It's the end goal that automation technologies like OCR and robotic process automation are often working toward, aiming to remove manual touchpoints from routine, high-volume transactions entirely.
examples: Straight through processing issued the policy the moment the application was submitted.
STP handled routine claims end to end, freeing adjusters to focus on complex cases.
Straight through processing rates became a key efficiency metric the insurer tracked closely.
Not every transaction qualified for straight through processing — some still needed a human check.
STP reduced data entry errors that used to creep in during manual handoffs between systems.

terms.definition: Additional coverage options added to a basic insurance policy to protect against risks not covered under the standard policy, letting a policyholder tailor coverage to their own needs. It functions similarly to an endorsement or rider, extending protection beyond a policy's base terms to address a specific gap or need the standard coverage doesn't fully fill.
examples: Supplementary coverage for jewelry filled the gap the standard homeowners policy left.
The agent recommended supplementary coverage for water backup, since the base policy excluded it.
Supplementary coverage comes at an added premium on top of the base policy.
Reviewing the policy each year helped identify where supplementary coverage might be worth adding.
Supplementary coverage options vary widely from one insurer's base policy to another's.

terms.definition: Artificially generated data created through algorithms or simulations that mimics the statistical properties of real data, used in insurance for modeling and analysis when real data is limited or sensitive. This approach lets insurers develop and test models without exposing sensitive real customer data, or in situations where genuine historical data is too sparse to train a reliable model on its own.
examples: Synthetic data let the fraud team test its model without exposing any real customer records.
The insurer generated synthetic data to model a new product for which it had no actual claims history yet.
Synthetic data in insurance has to be validated carefully to make sure it reflects real-world patterns.
Using synthetic data sidestepped some of the privacy concerns tied to training on real claims data.
Synthetic data supplemented the small sample of real claims for a newly launched line of business.

terms.term: Technology Errors and Omissions (Tech E&O) Insurance
terms.definition: Insurance covering technology companies and professionals against claims of negligence or inadequate work related to technology services or products, covering both liability and property loss exposures. It's a specialized variant of professional errors and omissions coverage, tailored to the specific risks technology companies face, like a software bug causing a client financial loss.
examples: Tech E&O insurance covered the software vendor after a bug allegedly caused a client's financial loss.
The consulting firm couldn't sign the contract without proof of technology errors and omissions insurance.
Tech E&O insurance is written specifically around technology work, unlike general professional liability.
A missed deadline that caused a client financial harm was exactly the kind of claim Tech E&O insurance was meant for.
Underwriting Tech E&O insurance meant understanding the specific software or service the company provided.

terms.definition: The principle of providing clear, accessible, and understandable information about policies, coverage, and the claims process, so policyholders can make informed decisions. Greater transparency helps build trust and reduces disputes, since a policyholder who clearly understood what they were buying is less likely to feel blindsided by a claim outcome later.
examples: Transparency in insurance meant the policy plainly listed what wasn't covered, not just what was.
Digital engagement tools improved transparency in insurance by letting customers track a claim's status live.
Regulators pushed for greater transparency in insurance pricing after complaints about hidden fees.
Transparency in insurance built trust with customers who'd previously felt confused by their coverage.
The insurer's plain-language policy summary was part of a broader push for transparency in insurance.

terms.definition: Insurance covering medical expenses, trip cancellation, lost luggage, and other losses incurred while traveling, purchasable for a single trip or on a multi-trip basis for frequent travelers. It's closely related to the broader travel coverage category, though this term more specifically refers to the standalone insurance product travelers purchase for a trip.
examples: Travel insurance reimbursed the cost of the canceled flight after the family emergency.
She bought travel insurance mainly for the medical coverage while traveling abroad.
Travel insurance covered the lost luggage, though it took a few weeks to process.
Frequent travelers often find an annual multi-trip travel insurance plan cheaper than buying per trip.
Travel insurance policies vary widely in what counts as a covered reason for trip cancellation.

terms.definition: The part of a blockchain system that ensures the integrity and security of transactions and data exchanges across the network, eliminating the need for a central authority through distributed consensus and a tamper-proof ledger. This distributed trust mechanism is what allows unrelated parties, like an insurer, reinsurer, and claimant, to rely on a shared record without needing to trust each other, or a single central authority, directly.
examples: The trust layer in blockchain made it possible for several insurers to share claims data without a central intermediary.
Smart contracts rely on the trust layer in blockchain to execute reliably without a third party.
The trust layer in blockchain gave all parties confidence the shared ledger hadn't been altered.
Explaining the trust layer in blockchain to non-technical stakeholders took some simplifying.
The trust layer in blockchain is what lets decentralized identity verification work in insurtech pilots.

terms.definition: A risk that falls outside what an insurance company deems acceptable to cover, either because a loss is too likely, prohibited by law, or too large or difficult to quantify. Risks falling into this category are typically addressed through other means entirely, like government programs, self-insurance, or simply accepting the exposure, since no commercial insurer is willing to take them on.
examples: The underwriter declined the account, calling the exposure an uninsurable risk.
War is a classic example of an uninsurable risk excluded from most standard policies.
A risk that's already occurring, like an ongoing lawsuit, is generally treated as an uninsurable risk.
What counts as an uninsurable risk can shift over time as insurers develop new ways to price it.
The business had to self-insure the uninsurable risk since no carrier would take it on.

terms.definition: The overall experience of using an insurtech platform or application, especially how easy and pleasant it is to use — a critical factor in engaging customers and simplifying digital insurance processes. Strong UX has become a genuine competitive differentiator in insurtech, since a clunky or confusing digital experience can undermine even a well-priced, well-designed insurance product.
examples: Poor UX in the claims app was the top complaint in customer feedback surveys.
The insurtech's UX in insurtech design let a first-time user buy a policy in under two minutes.
Improving user experience in insurtech directly reduced how many customers abandoned the signup flow.
UX research revealed customers didn't understand a key step in the online claims process.
Good UX in insurtech means making a complicated product feel simple, not making it simpler than it is.

terms.definition: A statistical technique measuring the potential loss on a portfolio of financial assets over a given period at a certain confidence level. Insurers use VaR to estimate potential losses and set capital reserves. While widely used, this measure has known limitations, since it doesn't capture how severe losses could be beyond the specified confidence level, which is why it's often used alongside other risk measures.
examples: The investment team calculated Value at Risk to gauge how much the portfolio could lose in a bad month.
A 99% VaR meant losses were expected to exceed that threshold only 1% of the time.
VaR informed how much capital the insurer set aside against its investment portfolio.
Value at Risk has real limitations for estimating extreme, rare events like a market crash.
The risk committee reviewed VaR figures alongside other capital adequacy metrics.

terms.definition: Telecommunications and informatics embedded directly in a vehicle — GPS navigation, hands-free systems, wireless safety communications, driving assistance — used in insurance to assess driver behavior and support usage-based pricing. This broader telematics infrastructure is what makes usage-based insurance pricing possible, translating a vehicle's actual, observed use into data an insurer can price against.
examples: Vehicle telematics built into the new car reported driving data automatically, with no separate app needed.
The manufacturer's vehicle telematics system fed data directly to the insurer with the owner's consent.
Vehicle telematics tends to capture more consistent data than a phone-based app does.
Vehicle telematics data helped reconstruct exactly what happened in the seconds before the crash.
Vehicle telematics adoption grew as more new cars shipped with the hardware built in.

terms.definition: Investment funds allocated to early-stage insurtech startups with high growth potential, funding the technology-driven innovation that's reshaping how insurance is priced, sold, and serviced. This funding has fueled much of the innovation reshaping the industry, though insurtech startups still ultimately need to navigate the same regulatory and capital requirements as traditional insurers to actually sell coverage.
examples: Venture capital in insurtech funded the startup's first three years before it turned profitable.
A surge of venture capital in insurtech in one year was followed by a much quieter funding environment the next.
Investors providing venture capital in insurtech often looked for a clear path to partnering with an established insurer.
Venture capital in insurtech dried up for startups that couldn't show a credible underwriting model.
The venture capital in insurtech that the company raised went mostly toward building its claims technology.

terms.definition: An AI-driven chatbot or virtual assistant designed to simulate a human insurance agent's advice and service, guiding customers through policy selection, answering questions, and assisting with claims around the clock. It's often built on the same conversational AI technology underlying broader insurance chatbots, but positioned specifically as a substitute for the advisory role a human agent traditionally plays.
examples: The virtual insurance agent walked her through choosing between two coverage options.
A virtual insurance agent handled the initial claims intake before a human adjuster took over.
The virtual insurance agent was available at 2 a.m. when the real agent's office was closed.
Some customers still asked to be transferred from the virtual insurance agent to a person.
The virtual insurance agent's recommendations were based on the same underwriting rules a human agent would use.

terms.definition: The process of identifying, classifying, and prioritizing vulnerabilities in computer systems, applications, and networks. In cyber insurance, vulnerability assessments help underwriters understand a business's cyber exposure. This kind of technical assessment gives underwriters a much more concrete basis for pricing cyber risk than relying on a business's own self-reported security practices alone.
examples: The vulnerability assessment found an unpatched server that had been exposed for months.
Cyber insurers increasingly require a vulnerability assessment before quoting larger accounts.
The vulnerability assessment ranked findings by severity so the IT team could prioritize fixes.
A clean vulnerability assessment supported a lower premium at renewal.
The vulnerability assessment became part of the insurer's standard cyber underwriting checklist.

terms.definition: Electronic devices worn by individuals that collect and analyze personal data, including health and fitness information. In insurance, wearables are used to monitor policyholder health metrics, encourage healthy behavior, and personalize life and health premiums. This kind of continuous, real-world health data represents a significant shift from traditional life and health underwriting, which historically relied on a single point-in-time medical exam or questionnaire.
examples: Wearable technology tracked her daily steps, which qualified her for a wellness discount.
The life insurer's wearable technology program rewarded consistent exercise with lower premiums.
Wearable technology raised questions about how health data collected for a discount program would be used.
Wearable technology data supplemented, rather than replaced, the standard health questionnaire.
Adoption of wearable technology programs was highest among younger, more health-conscious policyholders.

terms.definition: Financial instruments used to hedge against losses tied to weather conditions, offered as an alternative or complement to traditional insurance for risks like drought, excessive rainfall, or temperature swings. Because payout is based on a measurable weather index rather than actual proven loss, this instrument functions similarly in spirit to parametric insurance, just structured as a financial derivative rather than a traditional policy.
examples: The farm cooperative used weather derivatives to hedge against a poor growing season.
Weather derivatives paid out based on a measured weather index, not an assessed loss.
A ski resort bought weather derivatives to offset revenue lost during a low-snowfall winter.
Weather derivatives settle faster than a traditional claim, since the trigger is just a weather reading.
Weather derivatives and parametric insurance share a similar trigger-based structure.

terms.definition: An online platform that gathers and presents insurance products and prices from multiple insurers, letting consumers compare coverage options in one place. While convenient for consumers, these platforms have also increased pricing competition and transparency across the industry, since it's now easier than ever to compare options across insurers directly.
examples: She used a web aggregator to compare auto quotes from five insurers at once.
The web aggregator earned a commission whenever a comparison led to a purchased policy.
Insurers had to decide whether listing on a web aggregator was worth the price competition it invited.
A web aggregator simplified shopping but didn't always show every coverage detail side by side.
Web aggregators pushed some insurers to compete more directly on price.

terms.definition: The recognition that an insured item, such as a vehicle or property, is a total loss and not worth repairing, because the repair cost exceeds the item's value or it's irreparably damaged. It's essentially the everyday term for what's more formally described as a total loss, or a constructive total loss when technical repair remains possible but isn't economically sensible.
examples: The insurer declared the car a write-off once repair estimates came in above its market value.
A write-off pays out the item's value instead of funding repairs.
The homeowner disputed the write-off, arguing the house could still be salvaged.
Older vehicles are more likely to be a write-off after even moderate damage.
Once a car is a write-off, its salvage title follows it for the rest of its life.

terms.definition: A term life insurance policy renewed annually, allowing the insured to renew each year without proving insurability again, though premiums typically rise with age. Because coverage renews without new medical underwriting, this structure guarantees continued insurability, though the rising annual cost as the insured ages eventually makes it less economical than other permanent alternatives for long-term coverage.
examples: YRT let him keep renewing coverage each year without a new medical exam.
Yearly renewable term premiums climbed noticeably once he passed sixty.
YRT suits someone who needs short-term coverage with the flexibility to extend it.
The reinsurer priced the yearly renewable term treaty based on a standard mortality table.
Yearly renewable term is often used as a rider rather than as someone's primary life coverage.

terms.definition: The earnings generated on an insurance company's investments over a given period, expressed as a percentage of the investment's cost, helping offset claims costs and support the insurer's overall financial health. A stronger investment yield can help offset a weaker underwriting result, which is one reason insurers sometimes accept an underwriting loss if they expect investment returns to more than make up the difference.
examples: Bond yield improved the insurer's overall investment return for the year.
The portfolio's yield fell as older, higher-rate bonds matured and were replaced at lower rates.
A stable yield on the investment portfolio helped keep premiums more affordable.
The insurer's investment team was tasked with maximizing yield without taking on excessive risk.
Yield on invested premiums is a meaningful part of an insurer's overall profitability.

terms.term: Zero Trust Architecture in Cyber Insurance
terms.definition: A cybersecurity principle assuming no user or device should be automatically trusted, requiring continuous verification. Adopting zero trust architecture can lower an insured's cyber risk and, in turn, its cyber insurance premium. Insurers increasingly look for evidence of practices like this during underwriting, since a business with stronger baseline cybersecurity controls generally presents a lower expected claims cost.
examples: Adopting zero trust architecture helped the company qualify for a lower cyber insurance premium.
The cyber underwriter asked specifically whether the applicant had implemented zero trust architecture.
Zero trust architecture assumes a breach is possible and limits how far an attacker can move once inside.
Zero trust architecture in cyber insurance is increasingly treated as a baseline expectation, not a bonus.
Rolling out zero trust architecture across the company took over a year to complete.
lookup_keys: zero trust architecture in cyber insurance

terms.definition: A cyber-attack exploiting a software vulnerability on the same day it's discovered, before a patch exists. In cyber insurance, zero-day attacks represent a significant risk since businesses had no chance to defend against them in advance. Because no patch or defense exists at the moment of attack, this represents one of the harder cyber risks for a business to guard against proactively, and one insurers weigh carefully when pricing cyber coverage.
examples: The zero-day attack exploited a flaw no one, including the software vendor, had known about.
Cyber insurers price for the possibility of a zero-day attack even though it's impossible to predict.
The zero-day attack was patched within days, but not before several companies were compromised.
A zero-day attack claim tested how quickly the insurer's incident response team could mobilize.
Zero-day attacks are a reminder that even well-patched systems aren't fully protected.

terms.definition: The practice of setting insurance premiums and coverage options based on the geographic location of the insured, identified by zip code, factoring in crime rates, natural disaster risk, and other local conditions. This practice has drawn regulatory scrutiny in some jurisdictions, given concerns that geography-based pricing can sometimes correlate with, and effectively proxy for, factors regulators don't want reflected in insurance pricing.
examples: Zip code underwriting pushed her premium up when she moved to a higher-crime area.
Regulators scrutinized zip code underwriting for its potential to disproportionately affect certain communities.
Zip code underwriting is one input among several, not the only factor in the final rate.
The insurer's zip code underwriting model was updated after new flood maps were released.
Zip code underwriting can lead to noticeably different rates for otherwise similar applicants in different areas.

terms.definition: Local government regulations governing how land in a given area can be used, which insurers take into account when assessing property risk and the cost of rebuilding after a loss. Zoning classifications can directly affect what a property is even legally permitted to be rebuilt as after a total loss, which is why insurers and policyholders alike need to understand them before assuming a straightforward rebuild is possible.
examples: Zoning laws required the rebuilt structure to meet current code, adding cost the original policy hadn't anticipated.
The underwriter checked local zoning laws before quoting coverage for the mixed-use building.
Zoning laws can force a larger rebuild than the original structure if the property no longer conforms to current rules.
Ordinance or law coverage exists specifically to address gaps created by changing zoning laws.
Zoning laws varied enough between neighboring towns that the same claim would be handled differently.
